 TRANSMISSION OWNERS IN RESPONSE TO SEPTEMBER 28, 2026, ANSWER
                       OF COMPLAINANT

       Pursuant to Rule 213(a)(2) of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy

Regulatory Commission (“Commission”),1 the Ohio Transmission Owners 2 respectfully move

for leave to submit this answer in response to the September 28, 2026 Answer of Complainant

Office of the Ohio Consumers’ Counsel (“OCC”) 3 regarding OCC’s motion to expedite and to




       1
           18 C.F.R. § 385.213(a)(2) (2026).
       2
         The Ohio Transmission Owners are American Electric Power Service Corporation, on behalf
of Ohio Power Company and AEP Ohio Transmission Company (collectively, “AEP”), FirstEnergy
Service Company, as agent for its affiliate American Transmission Systems, Inc. (“ATSI”), The Dayton
Power and Light Company d/b/a AES Ohio (“AES Ohio”), and Duke Energy Ohio, Inc. (“Duke”).
       3
          Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer of the Office of the Ohio Consumers’ Counsel to
the Ohio Transmission Owners’ Answer to Motion to Expedite and Lodge Additional Information,
Docket No. 23-105-000 (Sept. 28, 2026).
 lodge.4 The Commission should accept the Ohio Transmission Owners’ answer because OCC

reports on the Attachment M-3 process only as of the date of OCC’s latest filing on September

28, 2026, and thus necessarily omits what has occurred since then. 5 Even worse, OCC neglects

to report on Duke’s responses that were posted six days before OCC’s filing. 6 The Commission

will benefit from learning of these materials posted in the Attachment M-3 process. They

demonstrate that the Attachment M-3 process is the appropriate forum for OCC to pose

questions and receive answers, and that there is no basis to declare unjust and unreasonable

that process or the other types of regulatory review currently in place for supplemental

transmission projects.

          Specifically, on September 22, 2026, six days before OCC’s most recent filing in this

Docket on September 28, 2026, PJM posted twelve responses by Ohio Transmission Owner

Duke in response to OCC’s questions. 7 OCC fails to mention Duke’s responses in its latest

filing.

          Additionally, on September 28, 2026, the same day as OCC’s latest filing in this

Docket, PJM posted twenty-four responses from AEP to OCC’s questions. 8 For example,

concerning Project No. AEP-2026-AP007, in response to OCC’s request for “[t]he planning

assumptions supporting the projected 1,000 MW customer load,” AEP explained that it

Consumers’ Counsel, Docket No. EL23-105-000 (Aug. 27, 2026).

the state of the Attachment M-3 process only as of August 27, 2026, as the Ohio Transmission Owners
explained in their answer filed on September 11, 2026. See Answer of the Ohio Transmission Owners
to Motion for Expedited Action and to Lodge New Information, Docket No. EL23-105-000 (Sept. 11,
2026).
          6

 “analyzed service to the customer using the 2030 RTEP cases and evaluated the load under the

AEP Connection Requirements for the AEP Transmission System. See AEP Assumptions

Slide 12.” 9

        The record demonstrates that the Attachment M-3 process worked as intended. OCC

raised questions regarding the referenced transmission projects, and the Ohio Transmission

Owners provided responsive information and explanations. To the extent OCC believes

additional information would be helpful, OCC may continue to avail itself of the Attachment

M-3 process to pose any follow-up questions, rather than asserting that the process itself is

unjust and unreasonable.

        WHEREFORE, for the foregoing reasons and those in the Ohio Transmission Owners’

prior submissions, the Commission should deny OCC’s motion to lodge, and in the alternative

should consider subsequent responses by Ohio Transmission Owners in the Attachment M-3

process.

On behalf of Duke Energy Ohio DEOK:

At the Needs and Solutions meeting held last month, OCC submitted several questions regarding
the Needs presentation for this project. To date, those questions have not been addressed.
OCC respectfully requests that Duke Energy Ohio provide written responses to the outstanding
questions before these projects proceed further in the planning process. The questions concern
matters central to evaluating the proposed projects, including the basis for the identified need,
underlying load forecast assumptions, customer commitments, consideration of alternatives,
project scope, timing, and expected consumer cost impacts.
As it pertains to the Solutions stage of the project, OCC requests the following additional
information:
1. What evidence supports the increase from 500MW to 800 MW?
Specifically, has the customer made a binding commitment for the additional 300 MW, and what is
the anticipated in-service schedule for that additional load?
        (DEOK) As described in the previous set of questions, DEO has one Electric Service
Agreement (ESA) executed for 250 MW. Additional requested load is still under review.

2. Has Duke evaluated scenarios in which only the original 500 MW materializes or the
additional 300 MW is delayed?
If so, would the same transmission upgrades still be required under those scenarios?
          (DEOK) The system upgrades necessary to bring the original 500 MW online were
identified during the Attachment M-3 Supplemental Project Do-No-Harm study process for DEOK-
2024-006. The newly identified transmission upgrades are required to supply the combination of
the originally studied-and-approved 500 MW load in addition to the requested 300 MW load
increase.
 3. How will Duke ensure that existing retail customers are not responsible for costs associated
with facilities built primarily to serve this customer’s increased load?
(DEOK) This question is focused on cost assignment and cost recovery, which goes beyond the
scope of planning information that DEOK is required to provide through the stakeholder process
pursuant to Attachment M-3. Notwithstanding that the question seeks information beyond the
scope of Attachment M-3, DEOK clarifies that electric service agreements are entered into so
data centers and other large customers pay for both the infrastructure needed to serve them and
their share of overall system costs. These contracts include long-term commitments and financial
safeguards – such as minimum billing requirements, upfront investments, credit support and
termination fees.

Response from Duke Energy Ohio (DEOK) Need number – Need No. DEOK-2026-004

OCC appreciates Duke Energy Ohio's presentation of Need No. DEOK-2026-004. Because this
project is being presented during the Needs stage of the M-3 process, OCC's comments focus on
whether Duke has adequately demonstrated the need for additional transmission facilities and
provided sufficient information for stakeholders to evaluate that need.

Duke Energy Ohio's presentation indicates that a customer previously requesting approximately
500 MW of load near Trenton, Ohio, now plans to increase its requested service by an additional
300 MW beginning in 2028.

Accordingly, OCC requests additional information regarding:

   1. The basis for the revised customer load forecast and what has changed since the prior
      need presentation.
DEOK: The customer load request has increased by 300 MW. This is the only change since
the prior Need presentation.

  1. Whether the additional load reflects expansion by the same customer or additional
     customer development.
DEOK: This additional load reflects expansion by the same customer.

   1. The level of customer commitment supporting the revised forecast, including executed
      service agreements and development milestones.
DEOK: DEO has one Electric Service Agreement (ESA) executed for 250 MW. Additional
requested load is still under review.
   1. The specific transmission planning criteria demonstrating the need for additional
      transmission facilities.
DEOK: The applicable transmission planning criteria is found in PJM Manual 14B: PJM
Region Transmission Planning Process, Section (2.3.8) “NERC P3 and P6 “N-1-1”
Analysis.
    1. Whether the identified need remains under lower customer load assumptions
DEOK: The scope of the proposed project is determined by the increased customer load. If
the increased load changes, the scope of the proposed project may or may not change.

  1. Whether future transmission facilities can be developed in phases corresponding to
     demonstrated customer commitments.
DEOK: Yes, depending upon the project.

   1. Does PJM and/or the transmission owner have any information as to whether the
      prospective load interconnection customer has submitted similarly sized project
      proposals in other locations on that transmission owner’s system, or in other
      transmission zones.
DEOK: While DEO does not currently have a similarly sized project proposal from this
customer, DEO does not have access to the information as to whether or not similar sized
projects exist in neighboring territories, and the customer may have similarly sized
projects underway within other transmission zones in PJM.

   1. Has PJM and/or the transmission owner conducted any analyses of the extent to
       which existing loads need the expansions being considered for the large load
       interconnection to serve their needs now or in the future. If so, please provide that
       information.
DEOK: PJM and DEO evaluate transmission system needs using planning models that
include existing load as well as forecasted load growth over the applicable planning
horizon. As part of the PJM Regional Transmission Expansion Plan (RTEP) process, PJM
performs power flow, short-circuit and stability analysis and evaluates the system against
applicable NERC planning criteria. While neither PJM nor DEO have performed a separate
analysis that allocates a specific percentage of the need for a given expansion between
new load and existing customers, it remains that the PJM RTEP identifies upgrades
needed for the operational, economic, and reliability requirements of all PJM customers,
and the models used for RTEP incorporate all forecasted loads – not merely the
incremental large load.
Because the identified need appears to arise from the expansion of a specific customer request,
OCC also requests an explanation of how resulting transmission investments will be planned and
funded consistent with cost-causation principles and how existing residential consumers will be
protected from costs attributable primarily to serving new large-load customers.
DEOK: DEO recognizes the importance of ensuring that transmission investments
associated with new large-load customers are planned and funded in a manner consistent
with applicable cost-causation principles and that existing customers remain protected
from costs attributable to directly serving new large loads. For regional transmission
facilities identified through the PJM planning process, cost responsibility is determined
 pursuant to applicable provisions of the PJM Open Access Transmission Tariff and FERC-
approved cost-allocation methodology. DEO will continue to coordinate with PJM and
applicable regulatory authorities to ensure cost-causation principles are followed in
accordance with applicable tariffs.

ATTACHMENT C
                  Questions Regarding Need No. AEP-2025-OH19 (Project)

Introduction

AEP provides the following responses to the questions that Ohio Consumers’ Counsel submitted
on August 14, 2026, regarding the Project presented at the August 4, 2026 PJM Transmission
Expansion Advisory Committee meeting. The questions are included for context, followed by
AEP’s responses.


Questions and Responses

   1. What specific planning assumptions changed since the original Need for this project
      was identified, and what new information prompted AEP to revise the existing need?

          a. The customer signed a new agreement for additional load at the identified
             location.

   2. How do the revised load forecasts, system conditions, or customer commitments compare
      with those supporting the original need, and what analysis demonstrate that the revised
      need is more accurate? Are there increased costs from the scope change?

          a. The customer signed a new agreement for additional load at this location. AEP will
             consider this increased load when presenting a solution to stakeholders.

   3. Did AEP evaluate whether the change in the identified need affects the scope, timing, or
      size of the proposed transmission solution, including whether a lower-cost or phased
      alternative is now appropriate?

          a. AEP has not yet presented a solution for the original need. When it does, the
             proposed solution will address the full scope of the need, including any
             alternatives considered. AEP studied the requested load reflected in the signed
